input.reason: All three baseline observations were unassisted and correct (accuracy 1.00, above the preregistered 0.70–1.00 band), and the predicted factor-pair overgeneralization never surfaced. But every item was tagged exposure=previously_practiced and provenance=practice, so this is rehearsed performance, not transfer. Practice cannot confirm the hypothesis; it can only justify the transfer test. Quest eligibility is met on independent correct evidence, so the correct move is to spend that eligibility on genuinely unseen material — missing-factor and equal-groups reasoning embedded in a situation the child has never met, where a factor must be recovered rather than recalled. The 43-second completion and 5/5 rating also say the baseline was too small to strain anything; the Quest should cost something.
preserve: Unassisted response capture with no scaffolds offered before an answer is committed
Short items that resolve in under a minute each, matching the pace that held attention
Concrete quantities the child can picture as groups of objects
Explicit per-item correctness so each response is a separate scored reading
change: Replace previously_practiced items with unseen contexts and unseen number pairs
Require recovering an unknown factor from a total and a group size, not just producing a product
Introduce a real cost for a wrong commitment instead of frictionless completion
Add word-problem framings where the wrong operation is plausibly available, to expose interpretation errors
Escalate quantities and remove the visible grid so grouping must be reasoned, not counted
testNext: Whether equal-groups reasoning survives a context never practiced
Whether missing-factor problems are solved by division/inverse reasoning rather than guess-and-check on memorized pairs
Whether factor-pair overgeneralization appears when the total has multiple valid factorizations and only one fits the situation
Whether accuracy holds when the answer cannot be found by counting visible objects
Whether a wrong answer that costs something triggers correction or shutdown
nextEvidenceRequired: At least 4 target-aligned unassisted observations tagged exposure=unseen
At least one missing-factor item where the total admits more than one factor pair and the context disambiguates
At least one word problem whose surface numbers invite addition instead of multiplication
Per-item response latency and any self-correction before commit
Error text captured verbatim for misconception scoping
input.nextAcademicTarget: math.multiplication.transfer — equal groups, missing factor, and word-problem interpretation applied to unseen contexts and unseen number pairs
input.nextMechanic: Loading run: the child fills ferry decks by choosing how many crates go in each row and how many rows, then sends the ferry across a river that is rising; each departure is timed by the water level, not a clock.
input.nextTheme: A night river crossing during a flood. Lanterns must reach the far village before the water swallows the dock. The child is the loader on the last ferry of the night.
input.nextOpeningPurpose: The first screen shows the dock already ankle-deep and one ferry left, with a dockmaster saying only: "Sixty lanterns. Eight to a crate. Tell me how many crates and I'll start hauling." No tutorial, no practice round — the child's first act is a real load decision that the ferry departs with.
input.nextCreatorPrompt: Build a five-crossing loading run for a nine-year-old on unseen multiplication transfer. Each crossing gives a total and one known part of the grouping, and the child must supply the missing part before the ferry can leave. Crossing 1: total lanterns and lanterns-per-crate given, child states crate count. Crossing 2: crates and per-crate given, child states total, but the deck only fits a set number of rows so the child must arrange as rows × columns. Crossing 3: a word problem where the dockmaster mentions two numbers that beg to be added ("nine villagers waiting, each needs four lanterns") — the correct move is multiplication. Crossing 4: a total that factors more than one way (e.g., 36) with a constraint that only one factor pair satisfies ("crates must fit six across the ramp"), so a memorized pair is not enough. Crossing 5: the deck grid is hidden under a tarp — no objects to count, the child must reason the missing factor from total and rows alone, with larger numbers than any earlier crossing. Every answer is committed by dragging the crate stack onto the ferry; once it's aboard, the ferry leaves. Capture each response verbatim, unassisted, with latency. No hints before commit; after a wrong crossing the dockmaster says what actually arrived and what didn't, then the water rises and the next crossing begins.
input.nextStakesDesign: Lanterns are the stake and they are spent, not scored. Every crossing the child under-loads, those lanterns stay on the dock and the flood takes them — the far village stays dark in that district, visibly, for the rest of the run. Over-load and the ferry swamps: the crates that sink are gone too. The child is playing to see how much of the village they can light, and the ending screen is the far shore as they actually left it — five districts lit, or three, or one. A wrong answer costs real, permanent, visible territory. It does not end the run, because the run's point is the shape of the shoreline at the end, and a child who lost district two should still be fighting for district five.
input.nextFailureMode: A run can end with the far village mostly dark. If three or more crossings are mis-loaded, the water reaches the dock before the fifth ferry and the last crossing never happens — the run ends early, with the remaining lanterns shown floating away and a count of how many people are still waiting in the dark. That is a real loss and it is presented as one.
input.nextEscalation: Crossing 1 is a clean total-and-part with a visible grid to check against. Crossing 2 adds a deck constraint so the grouping must be arranged, not just counted. Crossing 3 hides the multiplication inside language that invites addition. Crossing 4 makes the total ambiguous so a memorized factor pair fails without the constraint. Crossing 5 removes the visible objects entirely and raises the numbers past anything earlier — reasoning only, with the water at the child's knees and one ferry left.
input.nextMechanicSpec: The child drags a crate stack from the dock onto the ferry deck; a number pad sets crates-per-stack and a slider sets stack count, and the running lantern total is shown only as crates aboard — never as the answer. Tapping "Cast off" commits. On a correct load the ferry pulls out, the far shore lights up one district at a time as crates unload, and the water level drops a notch. On an under-load the ferry leaves anyway with a gap on the deck, the leftover crates are shown on the dock, and the flood pulls them into the current while the corresponding district on the far shore stays black. On an over-load the deck tilts, crates slide off the stern and sink with the lanterns going out one by one underwater. After every crossing the water line on screen rises by a fixed amount; at three failures it crosses the dock boards and the run ends there.
input.nextMathematicalHook: Thirty-six lanterns can be crated as 4×9, 6×6, or 12×3 — the arithmetic is equally true every way, and the ramp width is what decides which truth loads the ferry. The whoa is discovering that a number has several shapes, and the situation, not the multiplication table, picks the one that fits.
input.revisedHypothesis: Lab Learner can produce correct multiplication answers on rehearsed material; whether that reflects transferable equal-groups and missing-factor reasoning is untested, and will show most clearly when a total admits multiple factor pairs and only a situational constraint selects the right one.
